# Problem 1
##### The goal is to do some exploration of this dataset. To that end, write a short description of the dataset, noting the size and structure of the data, describing some key variables, and indicating the extent to which missing data is an issue. 
```{r}
data("ny_noaa")
```

The NY NOAA dataset include weather data from all New York state weather stations from January 1, 1981 through December 31, 2020, from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association. The dataset include `r nrow(ny_noaa)` daily weather observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables. Two of the variables serve as identifiers, including a character identifier for the weather station and a date of the daily weather observation at that station. Weather measurements include precipitation (tenths of millimeters), snowfall (millimeters), snow depth (millimeters), maximum temperature (tenths of degrees Celsius), and minimum temperature (tenths of degrees Celsius). While the dataset is tidy in structure, there is extensive missingness among the measurement variables, as each weather station may not had collected all five measurements. Of the `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations, missingness occurred for `r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, prcp)))` precipitation measurements, `r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, snow)))` snowfall measurements, `r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, snwd)))` snow depth measurements, `r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmax)))` maximum temperature measurements, and `r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmin)))` minimum temperature measurements. 

##### Do some data cleaning. Create separate variables for year, month, and day. Ensure observations for temperature, precipitation, and snowfall are given in reasonable units. For snowfall, what are the most commonly observed values? Why?
```{r}
ny_noaa_clean = ny_noaa |> 
  filter(!is.na(prcp) | !is.na(snow) | !is.na(snwd) | !is.na(tmax) | !is.na(tmin)) |> 
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    prcp = prcp / 10, 
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
    ) |> 
  relocate(id, date, year, month, day, everything()) 

ny_noaa_clean |> 
  group_by(snow) |> 
  summarize(count = n()) |> 
  arrange(desc(count))
```

Data cleaning first involved removing any observations in which all five weather measurements were missing. Next, I generated the year, month, and day for of each measurement date. Finally, the minimum and maximum temperatures were stored as character type, which I converted to numeric type. Furthermore, the minimum and maximum temperatures were stored in unintuitive units, tenths of degrees Celsius, such that I divided by ten so that the unit would then be degrees Celsius; I did the same for precipitation which was stored as tenths of millimeters.  

The most commonly observed values for snowflake, other than missing, were 0 millimeters (n=2008508), 25 millimeters (n=31022), and 13 millimeters (n=23095). Those measurements correspond to approximately 0, 1, and 0.5 inches, respectively, which makes sense as to why they are the most commonly observed.

##### Make a two-panel plot showing the average max temperature in January and in July in each station across years. Is there any observable / interpretable structure? Any outliers? 
```{r, message = FALSE}
ny_noaa_clean |> 
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7,
         !is.na(tmax)) |> 
  group_by(id, month, year) |> 
  summarize(tmax_avg = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(month = case_when(
    month == 1 ~ "January",
    month == 7 ~ "July"
    )) |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_boxplot(mapping = aes(x = year, y = tmax_avg, group = year)) + 
  facet_grid(~month) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July in Each Weather Station", 
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum \n Temperature (Celsius)"
    ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1980, 2010, 5))
```

This boxplot illustrates the distribution of average maximum temperature in January or July for each weather station across years. There are a few interesting observations. First, the median average temperature is more variable over time in January than July. That difference in variability could reflect how the average maximum temperature for weather stations downstate versus upstate New York are more aligned in July than January. Second, the distribution of average temperature in January appears by inspection to be shifting to warmer temperatures over time. The distribution in July does not appear to be changing. Finally, whereas the outliers in July are exclusively lower-tail outliers, the outliers in January are lower- and upper-tail outliers. Therefore, an unusually cold day in July may be considered an outlier, while an unusually cold or warm day in January may be considered an outlier. 

##### Make a two-panel plot showing (i) tmax vs tmin for the full dataset (note that a scatterplot may not be the best option); and (ii) showing the distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year.
```{r}
tmax_tmin = ny_noaa_clean |> 
  filter(!is.na(tmin) | !is.na(tmax)) |> 
  select(tmin, tmax) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    tmin:tmax, 
    names_to = "measurement",
    names_prefix = "t",
    values_to = "temperature"
    ) |> 
  filter(!is.na(temperature)) |> 
  mutate(measurement = case_when(
    measurement == "min" ~ "Minimum \n Temperature",
    measurement == "max" ~ "Maximum \n Temperature"
    )) |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_boxplot(mapping = aes(y = measurement, x = temperature)) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Minimum and Maximum Temperature", 
    x = "Temperature (Celsius)",
    y = "Measurement"
    )

snowfall = ny_noaa_clean |> 
  filter(snow > 0 & snow < 100) |> 
  group_by(year) |> 
  summarize(number_of_snowfalls = n()) |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_col(mapping = aes(x = year, y = number_of_snowfalls)) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Snowfalls Greater than 0 and Less than 100 Millimeters", 
    x = "Year",
    y = "Number of Snowfalls"
    ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1980, 2010, 5))

tmax_tmin / snowfall
```

This two-panel plot illustrates the (1) distribution of minimum and maximum temperature across the entire dataset, and (2) distribution of snowfalls greater than 0 and less than 100 millimeters. For the temperature boxplot, as expected, the distribution of maximum temperature is greater than minimum temperature, with lower- and upper-tail outliers for both. For the snowfalls histogram, the number of snowfalls greater than 0 and less than 100 millimeters was stable around 5000 per year from 1980 to 2006, but since 2006 has increased rapidly, exceeding 10000 in 2010. 

# Problem 2

##### Load, tidy, merge, and otherwise organize the data sets. Your final dataset should include all originally observed variables; exclude participants less than 21 years of age, and those with missing demographic data; and encode data with reasonable variable classes (i.e. not numeric, and using factors with the ordering of tables and plots in mind).
```{r, message = FALSE}
nhanes_covar <- read_csv("Data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(
    sex = case_when(
      sex == 1 ~ "Male",
      sex == 2 ~ "Female"
      ),
    education = case_when(
      education == 1 ~ "Less than high school",
      education == 2 ~ "High school equivalent",
      education == 3 ~ "More than high school"
      ),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("Male", "Female")),
    education = factor(education, levels = c("Less than high school", 
                                             "High school equivalent",
                                             "More than high school"))
    ) |> 
  filter(age >= 21, 
         !is.na(bmi),
         !is.na(age)
         )

nhanes_accel <- read_csv("Data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |> 
  mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute))

nhanes <- inner_join(nhanes_accel, nhanes_covar, by = "seqn") |> 
  relocate(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education)
```

##### Produce a reader-friendly table for the number of men and women in each education category, and create a visualization of the age distributions for men and women in each education category. Comment on these items.
```{r, message = FALSE}
nhanes |> 
  select(seqn, sex, education) |> 
  unique() |> 
  group_by(sex, education) |>
  summarize(
    count = n()
  ) |> 
  knitr::kable()

nhanes |> 
  select(seqn, sex, age, education) |> 
  unique() |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_boxplot(mapping = aes(x = age, y = sex)) + 
  facet_wrap(~education) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(
    x = "Age (Years)",
    y = "Sex",
    title = "Distribution of Age by Sex and Education"
  )
```

##### Traditional analyses of accelerometer data focus on the total activity over the day. Using your tidied dataset, aggregate across minutes to create a total activity variable for each participant. Plot these total activities (y-axis) against age (x-axis); your plot should compare men to women and have separate panels for each education level. Include a trend line or a smooth to illustrate differences. Comment on your plot.
```{r, message = FALSE}
nhanes |> 
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |> 
  summarize(mims_total = sum(mims)) |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = age, y = mims_total, color = sex)) + 
  geom_smooth(mapping = aes(x = age, y = mims_total, color = sex), se = FALSE) + 
  facet_wrap(~education) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(
    x = "Age (Years)",
    y = "Total Activity (MIMS)",
    title = "Total Activity by Sex and Education"
  ) + 
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_blank()
  )
```

##### Accelerometer data allows the inspection activity over the course of the day. Make a three-panel plot that shows the 24-hour activity time courses for each education level and use color to indicate sex. Describe in words any patterns or conclusions you can make based on this graph; including smooth trends may help identify differences.
```{r, message = FALSE}
nhanes |> 
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_smooth(mapping = aes(x = minute, y = mims, color = sex), se = FALSE) +

  theme_minimal() +

    x = "Minutes of Day (0 is Midnight, 1440 is 11:59pm)",
    y = "Activity (MIMS)",
    title = "Total Activity by Sex and Education"
  ) + 
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_blank()
  )
```
